questions.statement: The classrooms ___ by the janitor every morning.
questions.context: The janitor arrives before the students every morning in the Ecuadorian school.

options.feedback: No. 'clean' is the active verb of the janitor, so the sentence says the janitor does it. The passive needs 'are cleaned', because the action is emphasised, not the doer.
Correct! Present simple passive is 'are' plus the past participle, and the subject 'the classrooms' is plural, so 'are cleaned' is the only form that fits.
No. 'is cleaned' is singular and the subject here is 'the classrooms'. Choosing it would break the agreement in number between subject and auxiliary.
No. 'have cleaned' is active and perfect, and it would make the classrooms the doer. Nothing in the sentence is doing the cleaning; the action matters, not the agent.

questions.explanation:
The passive voice is built with the auxiliary 'be' plus the past participle of the main verb. In the present simple the auxiliary takes the plural form 'are' when the subject is plural, and the tense and number of the action stay visible even though the doer has disappeared.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The new library ___ in our school right now.
questions.context: Construction of a new library is happening at the moment the announcement is read.

options.feedback: No. 'is built' is present simple passive. The adverb 'right now' asks for an action in progress, which needs the continuous form.
No. 'was built' places the construction in the past, but nothing in the sentence refers to a finished past action.
Correct! Present continuous passive is 'is being' plus the past participle, and it describes a construction that is happening at this moment.
No. 'has been built' presents the construction as a finished result relevant now. Here the emphasis is on the process still going on, not on the completed building.

questions.explanation:
When the action itself is in progress, English uses the continuous passive: auxiliary 'be' in the present plus 'being' plus the past participle. The two auxiliaries carry the aspect, so the process stays visible without naming the workers who are doing it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The bridge ___ to traffic in 1998.
questions.context: The Rio Balao bridge opened to traffic in 1998 after months of repairs.

options.feedback: Correct! Past simple passive is 'was' plus the past participle 'opened', which is exactly what a finished event in 1998 requires.
No. 'was opening' is a past continuous form and would describe an unfinished action, but the opening of the bridge was a single completed event.
No. 'were' is plural and the subject 'the bridge' is singular. The verb 'open' does not change the number agreement in this passive.
No. 'had opened' is active past perfect: the bridge would be doing the opening. The action here is received, not performed.

questions.explanation:
The past simple passive takes the singular auxiliary 'was' with the past participle, and it is used for a completed action in a finished past time. No agent is mentioned because the date and the event are what matter, not who was responsible.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The documents ___ by the customs officers when the alarm sounded.
questions.context: Customs officers were inspecting the documents at the airport when the alarm sounded.

options.feedback: No. 'were inspected' is past simple passive and presents the inspection as finished. The clause 'when the alarm sounded' shows it was still running.
No. 'are inspected' is present simple passive and would place the inspection now, but the whole story takes place in the past.
No. 'have been inspected' is present perfect passive and links the inspection to the present, which is not the time frame of the sentence.
Correct! Past continuous passive is 'were being' plus the past participle, and it matches an inspection that was in progress when the alarm interrupted it.

questions.explanation:
A past action that was running at a past moment is described with the past continuous passive: 'were' plus 'being' plus the past participle. The temporal clause 'when the alarm sounded' anchors the interruption, and the passive keeps the focus on the documents rather than on the officers.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The historic centre of Quito ___ by millions of visitors.
questions.context: Millions of people have visited the historic centre of Quito over the last decades.

options.feedback: No. 'has visited' makes the historic centre the visitor. The subject receives the action, so it needs a passive form with 'has been'.
No. 'had visited' is active past perfect and again gives the subject the role of the doer, which contradicts the meaning.
Correct! Present perfect passive is 'has been' plus the past participle, which links a past action to a present result without giving a date.
No. 'was visiting' is an active past continuous and would require the historic centre to be doing the visiting, which is impossible.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive joins a past event to the present with 'has been' plus the past participle. It is the tense English uses when the result matters now but the date of the action is irrelevant or unknown, exactly the situation when counting visitors over decades.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The exam results ___ tomorrow morning.
questions.context: The results of the national exam will be published the day after the session ends.

options.feedback: No. 'announce' is an active base form with no auxiliary. A passive sentence must show the tense with 'will be' plus a past participle.
Correct! Future simple passive is 'will be' plus the past participle, and 'tomorrow morning' fixes the publication in the future.
No. 'are announced' is present simple passive and would mean the results come out every morning, which contradicts 'tomorrow'.
No. 'will announce' is the future active and would make the exam results the ones doing the announcing.

questions.explanation:
The future simple passive is built with 'will be' followed by the past participle. It is the standard form for announcements of future events where the institution, not a named person, performs the action, so the agent can be left out.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The highway ___ next year, according to the approved plan.
questions.context: The provincial government has already approved funding for the highway repair.

options.feedback: No. 'will repair' is the future active and makes the highway the doer of the repair, which is not what the sentence states.
No. 'is repairing' is present continuous active and would claim that the repair is happening now.
No. 'repaired' has no auxiliary at all, so it carries neither tense nor voice. English requires a form of 'be' in every passive.
Correct! The passive of 'going to' is 'is going to be' plus the past participle, and it expresses a plan already decided for a future date.

questions.explanation:
Plans and schedules are often expressed with 'going to', and the passive of that construction is 'is going to be' plus the past participle. The reference to an approved plan confirms the intention exists, which is exactly the meaning of the 'going to' future.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The grammar handbook ___ by every student in this course.
questions.context: The grammar handbook is a text that every student in the course is able to consult.

options.feedback: Correct! Modal 'can' plus 'be' plus the past participle forms the modal passive, and it expresses what everybody is able to do with the handbook.
No. 'can read' is the modal active and would make the handbook the reader. The real subject of 'can' here is the student, not the book.
No. 'is read' is present simple passive and states a habit, without any reference to what students are capable of doing.
No. 'was read' is past simple passive and would claim the reading happened in the past, which the sentence never mentions.

questions.explanation:
Modal passives keep the modal unchanged and add 'be' before the past participle: can, could, may, might, must, should and would all behave this way. The structure expresses ability, permission or obligation about an action that is received rather than performed.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: If the road ___ , the accident could have been avoided.
questions.context: The road had not been closed that night, so the accident was unavoidable.

options.feedback: No. 'had closed' is the active past perfect and would make the road the element that closes itself, which is not something a road can do.
No. 'would close' is the modal active form of the condition and keeps the agent, so it does not belong in a passive conditional.
Correct! Third conditional passive is 'had been' plus the past participle, and it describes an unreal past condition that would have changed the outcome.
No. 'has been closing' is present perfect continuous, which is active and refers to an action that started in the past and is still going on.

questions.explanation:
An unreal condition in the past uses the third conditional, and its passive is built with 'had been' plus the past participle. The result clause uses 'could have been' plus participle, so both halves of the sentence are passive when the focus falls on the road and on the accident rather than on the people involved.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The library rules ___ at all times.
questions.context: Library rules apply to every reader, and breaking them is not tolerated at any time.

options.feedback: No. 'must respected' skips the form of 'be' entirely, which is ungrammatical in the passive. English needs 'must be respected'.
Correct! 'must be' plus the past participle is the modal passive of obligation, and 'at all times' reinforces that the rule has no exception.
No. 'are respected' is present simple passive and expresses a custom, not the strong obligation that 'at all times' signals here.
No. 'must respect' is the modal active, which would make the rules the ones doing the respecting instead of the ones being respected.

questions.explanation:
Obligation in the passive is expressed as 'must be' plus the past participle. The modal 'must' stays in front, the auxiliary 'be' appears immediately before the participle, and the resulting phrase describes a rule that is imposed on the reader rather than chosen by the reader.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: At the ceremony the mayor ___ a recognition for her work in the community.
questions.context: At the ceremony the mayor received a recognition on behalf of the whole community.

options.feedback: No. 'gives' is the simple present active, but the recognition arrives at the ceremony; it is not something the mayor hands out while speaking.
No. 'has given' makes the mayor the giver of the recognition and marks the action as completed, which reverses the meaning.
No. 'is giving' is present continuous active and again puts the mayor in the role of the person performing the action.
Correct! Past simple passive 'was given' puts the mayor in the role of the receiver, which is the whole point of choosing the passive in this sentence.

questions.explanation:
Choosing the passive changes the focus from the performer to the receiver. In a past event such as a ceremony, 'was given' highlights what the mayor received, while the person who actually handed over the recognition does not need to be named at all.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: There is nothing ___ about the damage to the wall.
questions.context: Nothing useful can be done about the damage, because the owner has left the city.

options.feedback: Correct! The passive infinitive 'to be done' is required after 'there is nothing', because the wall is the thing affected and not the one acting.
No. 'to do' is the active infinitive and would make the wall the element that does something, which contradicts 'nothing'.
No. 'doing' is a gerund form and cannot complete the structure 'there is nothing' without a form of 'be' before the participle.
No. 'done' alone has no infinitive marker and no auxiliary, so the phrase 'there is nothing done' is not a grammatical passive construction.

questions.explanation:
The construction 'there is nothing' followed by a gerund or an infinitive is common in English, and it always takes the passive form when the subject of the following action is the thing that is affected. The wall cannot be repaired by itself, so 'to be done' is the only coherent option.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: According to the report, the windows ___ during the night.
questions.context: Passengers reported that the windows of the bus had been broken during the night.

options.feedback: No. 'broke' is the active past simple and makes the windows the agents of the action. Windows cannot break windows.
No. 'are breaking' is present continuous active and describes a continuing action, which contradicts 'during the night'.
Correct! Past simple passive 'were broken' matches the plural subject 'the windows' and the past time expression 'during the night'.
No. 'have broke' is grammatically wrong because the past participle of break is 'broken', not 'broke'.

questions.explanation:
The subject 'the windows' receives the action, so the passive is required, and the plural noun demands the plural auxiliary 'were'. Past simple passive sentences with 'were' plus participle are the normal way English reports damage to objects without naming who caused it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When ___ the documents transferred to the national archive?
questions.context: An archivist wants to know the exact date when the documents were transferred.

options.feedback: No. 'did' is the auxiliary of the active; it needs a subject and a verb after it, and it cannot open a passive question on its own.
Correct! A passive question is formed with the subject first, then the auxiliary 'were' plus the past participle, which yields the interrogative word order 'were the documents transferred'.
No. 'was' is singular and the subject 'the documents' is plural. The number agreement must be respected even in an inverted question.
No. 'have' works with participle forms in perfect tenses but does not invert into a passive question about a definite past date such as this one.

questions.explanation:
Passive questions keep the normal English order of subject and auxiliary after the interrogative word: 'when were the documents transferred'. The auxiliary 'were' agrees with the plural subject, and the past participle closes the verb group exactly as it does in the affirmative.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The budget has not been approved, so the payment ___ this month.
questions.context: The committee has not approved the budget, so the payment cannot be made this month.

options.feedback: No. That form is possible in isolation, but the context describes a consequence of an unfinished approval in the present, which the present perfect passive negative expresses more directly.
No. 'was not made' places the failure in a closed past, while the sentence is about a situation that is still unresolved now.
No. 'is not being made' describes an action currently in progress, but nothing indicates that a payment is under way right now.
Correct! 'cannot be made' expresses the impossibility created by the missing approval, and the modal passive fits the causal link between the two clauses.

questions.explanation:
A modal passive expresses what is or is not possible as a result of a preceding fact. Here the unapproved budget makes the payment impossible, so 'cannot be made' is the form that expresses the consequence, keeping the payment in the role of the thing that is blocked.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly reports the move without naming the workers.
questions.context: The same goods were moved from one warehouse to another on two different dates.

options.text: The goods were moved to the second warehouse.
options.feedback: Correct! This is the past simple passive: the goods are the subject, they receive the action, and no worker is named, which is exactly what the instruction required.

options.text: The goods were moving to the second warehouse.
options.feedback: No. This is a past continuous passive, which would describe a movement still in progress. The report refers to a completed transfer between two warehouses.

options.text: The goods moved to the second warehouse.
options.feedback: No. This is the active past simple and it makes the goods the agents of their own transfer, which is semantically impossible.

options.text: The goods have moved to the second warehouse.
options.feedback: No. This is the active present perfect, so the goods perform the action, and it also links the move to the present in a way the report does not require.

questions.explanation:
Reporting an event without naming the agent obliges the author to use the passive. The past simple passive 'were moved' is the natural choice for a completed transfer described neutrally, and it keeps the sentence grammatical because the subject cannot perform the action.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The application needs ___ before it can be processed.
questions.context: The application must reach the office before it can be processed, and it needs a signature.

options.feedback: No. 'signing' is a gerund and belongs to a different construction. 'Needs' followed by a gerund describes a habitual action, not a single requirement.
Correct! 'needs to be signed' uses the passive infinitive because the application is the document that must receive the signature.
No. 'needs sign' is not grammatical after the modal-like verb 'need'; a form of 'be' plus participle is required in the passive.
No. 'needs being signed' mixes a gerund with a passive participle. English does not allow 'need' plus 'being' plus past participle here.

questions.explanation:
Verbs of requirement such as 'need', 'want' and 'must' are followed by an infinitive, and the infinitive becomes passive when the subject is the thing that receives the action. A form 'needs to be signed' therefore states clearly that the document, not a person, is the patient of the action.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The garden ___ by a volunteer every Saturday for years.
questions.context: A volunteer cleaned the garden every Saturday for years without anyone noticing.

options.feedback: Correct! The garden receives the action, so the past simple passive is right, and the agent appears only in the 'by' phrase as an optional detail.
No. 'cleaned' with no auxiliary has no tense and no voice. A bare past form cannot stand alone as the verb of a complete clause.
No. 'is cleaned' is present simple and would describe a habit that still continues, but the phrase 'for years' points to a period in the past.
No. 'has cleaned' is the active present perfect and would make the garden the person who cleans, which is exactly what a passive avoids.

questions.explanation:
The 'by' phrase is optional in English passives and works like a parenthesis that identifies the agent. Here it lets the reader know a volunteer did the work while the structure keeps the garden in focus, which is the whole advantage of choosing the passive voice.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The equipment ___ yet, and nobody knows who was responsible.
questions.context: Nobody has discovered who damaged the equipment in the laboratory during the night.

options.feedback: No. 'has been damaged' is grammatically correct, but the adverb 'yet' in a negative clause expects 'has not been damaged', so the sentence as written changes the meaning.
No. 'was damaged' presents the damage as a closed past event and cannot be combined with the negative adverb 'yet' in the way the sentence does.
Correct! The present perfect passive negative is 'has not been' plus the past participle, and 'yet' at the end fits that structure perfectly.
No. 'is not damaging' is active and would make the equipment the cause of the damage, which is the opposite of what the report says.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive negative takes 'has not been' plus the past participle, and the negative adverb 'yet' is placed at the end of the clause. The form links the unresolved damage to the present moment, which is why it goes with 'nobody knows who was responsible'.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The roof ___ with contributions from the whole province.
questions.context: The roof of the church was rebuilt with contributions from the whole province.

options.feedback: No. 'rebuilt' alone carries no auxiliary, so it can never form a complete clause in English. A passive needs an explicit form of 'be'.
No. 'has rebuilt' is the active present perfect and makes the roof the agent of its own reconstruction, which is not the intended meaning.
No. 'is building' is present continuous active and would mean the roof is performing the action at this moment.
Correct! 'was rebuilt' is the past simple passive, and the instrument phrase 'with contributions' explains how the rebuilding happened without naming a single agent.

questions.explanation:
The phrase 'with contributions' describes the means, not the agent, so it can follow a passive clause perfectly well. The past simple passive 'was rebuilt' matches the historical fact of a finished reconstruction, and the irregular participle 'rebuilt' is spelled exactly as the past simple here.
---
questions.subject: ingles
